newsitem.title: USA: New poll shows vast racial divide in U.S.
newsitem.headline: New poll shows vast racial divide in U.S.

text.p: A comprehensive new national poll shows that the racial divisions that President Bill Clinton hopes to bridge with his new initiative on social diversity are significant and persistent.

Conducted by the Gallup Organisation, the poll found that by a margin of 76 percent to 49 percent, more whites than blacks believe that blacks have equal opportunities for jobs, education and housing.

It also found blacks are twice as likely as whites to favour increasing affirmative action, the system of government preferences for minorities in hiring, contracts and schooling to make up for past discrimination.
Only in one area was there a convergence of views between the races -- 54 percent of whites and 58 percent of blacks said relations between them will always be a problem for the United States.
The poll was based on telephone interviews with 3,036 adults randomly selected from households throughout the country.

Clinton's new initiative, unveiled in a commencement speech at the University of California at San Diego, one of the country's most racially diverse campuses, is designed to be a hallmark of his presidency.

It also followed other empirical evidence of the U.S. racial divide, like the split between blacks and whites on the O.J. Simpson verdict. Most whites thought the former star athlete got away with murder when he was found innocent of killing former wife Nicole and her friend Ron Goldman; many blacks believed Simpson was framed by a biased justice system.

Clinton, who grew up in Arkansas at a time when racial segregation was practiced in the south, said on Friday that while conditions were "much better than they used to be," discrimination was still a problem.

"I think there is a real disparity in real opportunity, particularly for racial minorities who are physically isolated from the rest of us in low-income areas with high crime rates and low rates of economic and educational opportunity," he said.

In his second inaugural address, Clinton called on Americans to live up to the biblical injunction to be "healers of the breach," and White House aides described his race relations initiative as a follow-up.
But the initiative is broader than improving relations between blacks and whites. The U.S. population also includes increasing proportions of hispanics and Asian Americans.

"The greatest challenge we face is also our greatest opportunity. Can we become the world's first truly multi- racial, multi-ethnic democracy. Will we be one America in the 21st Century," Clinton asked in his speech.
